title: Diagnostics for Hemorrhagic Fever Viruses: Lassa Fever as an Example.
abstract: Lassa virus (LASV) causes severe hemorrhagic fever across West Africa where the development of rapid, accurate diagnostics remains hindered by the extensive lineage-level genetic diversity and by the limited availability of high-level containment laboratories. We developed a LASV assay using the CRISPR-based Streamlined Highlighting of Infections to Navigate Epidemics (SHINE) platform to enable safe, field-deployable detection. To enable assay development without handling live virus, we established a plasmid-based system that generates LASV RNA controls spanning major viral lineages. Using these surrogate plasmids, we optimized the assay for 32 genetically distinct LASV isolates, demonstrating detection across major lineage subdivisions with lineage-dependent sensitivity. The assay maintained sensitivity in serum and whole blood, and was further evaluated using clinical samples in Nigeria. To reduce subjectivity in strip interpretation, we developed supervised machine-learning models for automated classification of lateral flow results. Together, this integrated diagnostic framework supports field-oriented detection of genetically diverse LASV and provides a broader approach for diagnostic development for high-consequence RNA viruses.

title: Late-stage clinical development pathways for Lassa fever vaccines: scientific, operational, and regulatory considerations
abstract: Lassa fever remains a major public health challenge in West Africa, with recurring outbreaks and no licensed vaccine despite a growing pipeline. Low, seasonal incidence, and no identified biomarker of protection hinder traditional Phase 3 vaccine trials. Here, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) explores conventional and alternative clinical and regulatory pathways, with realistic evidence expectations for licensure, to advance Lassa vaccine candidates beyond Phase 2 where Phase 3 efficacy trials may not be feasible.

title: The role of Cbl-b: relationship between cancer and infectious disease
abstract: Casitas B-cell lymphoma-b protein (Cbl-b) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that negatively regulates signaling pathways. Although it is involved in the maintenance of immune homeostasis, Cbl-b may also be exploited by tumors or pathogens, leading to immune evasion and persistent infection. In recent years, the role of Cbl-b in tumor immunotherapy has been progressively elucidated, with related Cbl-b inhibitors (such as NX-1607) advancing into clinical trials. It has also been found that Cbl-b inhibition or knockout enhances host immune responses in infection models, such as lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) and Candida albicans infection models. Consequently, Cbl-b-targeting strategies hold promise as potent adjuncts to infectious disease treatments, particularly when combined with therapeutic vaccines or other immune-enhancing therapies. Given the immunological parallels between infection and tumorigenesis, this review examines the immunoregulatory role of Cbl-b in both contexts and compares their similarities and differences. Additionally, this review summarizes currently available mainstream Cbl-b-targeting strategies to provide new insights for the application of Cbl-b in immunotherapy for infectious diseases.

title: Progressive SLAMF7 downregulation is associated with terminal CD8 T-cell exhaustion and aggressive disease in renal cell carcinoma
abstract: T-cell exhaustion is a dysfunctional state under persistent antigenic stimulation in chronic viral infections and tumors. Although immune checkpoint blockade can reinvigorate exhausted T cells, responses remain limited, emphasizing the need to better understand exhaustion. SLAMF7 is an immune-regulatory receptor, but its regulatory and functional role during CD8 + T-cell exhaustion remains unclear. Here, we reported that SLAMF7 was absent in naïve mouse and human CD8 T cells but was induced upon in vitro activation. Following acute lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection, all effector and memory subsets expressed SLAMF7, with higher levels in more differentiated cytolytic populations. Under persistent antigenic stimulation, including chronic LCMV infection, murine tumor models, human renal cell carcinoma (RCC), and non-small cell lung cancer, SLAMF7 was highly expressed in progenitor and transitory exhausted subsets but downregulated in PD-1 hi terminally exhausted cells. This downregulation coincided with increased inhibitory receptor and TOX expression, attenuated cytotoxic and polyfunctional responses, and progressive epigenetic remodeling toward terminal exhaustion-associated chromatin programs. Furthermore, SLAMF7 deficiency impaired CD8 + T-cell expansion and antitumor activity. Across models, SLAMF7 downregulation was more closely associated with prolonged antigen exposure than with antigen burden. In RCC patients, SLAMF7-based stratification revealed distinct immunological states: SLAMF7-HI tumors retained progenitor-like CD8 T cells with preserved effector function, whereas SLAMF7-DN tumors were enriched for terminally exhausted cells and associated with high nuclear grade. Collectively, these findings identify SLAMF7 downregulation as a marker of terminal CD8 T-cell exhaustion and suggest its potential as a biomarker of immune competence and disease severity.

full_text: AbstractLymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV), a rodent-borne mammarenavirus, is endemic worldwide and under-appreciated although it has neurotropism and potential for serious clinical disease. LCMV is commonly carried by the house mouse (Mus musculus), thus being distributed globally in urban and rural areas. Transmission occurs primarily through inhalation of aerosolised excreta from infected rodents or contaminated secretions, with additional routes including solid organ transplantation, rarely, and vertical transmission. In humans, LCMV infection may vary from an inapparent or self-limiting febrile disease to more severe diseases such as aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis especially in immunocompromised patients. Congenital infections have been reported to cause chorioretinitis, intracranial calcifications, a variety of neurologic malformations, intellectual disability, neurodevelopmental problems, and death of the foetus. To date, 88 congenital cases of LCMV infection have been documented in the literature, and 5 donor-derived transplant-associated clusters involving 17 recipients have been reported worldwide. The objective of this narrative review is to provide a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of LCMV. Specifically, the review summarizes current knowledge on its virological characteristics, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Particular attention is given to congenital infection, transplant-associated disease, and the evolving epidemiology of LCMV, with emphasis on its public health relevance within a One Health framework. full_text: Zusammenfassung Arenaviren tragen ein segmentiertes RNA-Genom, das Leserahmen mit beiden Polaritäten enthält (Ambisense- Kodierungsstrategie). Die Viren werden von Nagetieren auf den Menschen übertragen und können schwere Erkrankungen auslösen. Das Lassa-Virus und weitere afrikanische und südamerikanische Arenaviren verursachen hämorrhagische Fieber mit zum Teil tödlichem Verlauf. Das Lymphozytäre Choriomeningitis-Virus (LCMV) kommt weltweit vor und kann bei immunkompetenten Personen eine aseptische Meningitis auslösen. Nach LCMV-Übertragung auf immunsupprimierte Patienten kommt es zu tödlichen Verläufen, die kongenitale Infektion kann zu Fehlbildungen des fetalen Gehirns führen. LCMV ist außerdem ein wichtiges Modellpathogen für immunologische Studien. Zusammenfassung Arenaviren tragen ein segmentiertes RNA-Genom, das Leserahmen mit beiden Polaritäten enthält (Ambisense- Kodierungsstrategie). Die Viren werden von Nagetieren auf den Menschen übertragen und können schwere Erkrankungen auslösen. Das Lassa-Virus und weitere afrikanische und südamerikanische Arenaviren verursachen hämorrhagische Fieber mit zum Teil tödlichem Verlauf. Das Lymphozytäre Choriomeningitis-Virus (LCMV) kommt weltweit vor und kann bei immunkompetenten Personen eine aseptische Meningitis auslösen. Nach LCMV-Übertragung auf immunsupprimierte Patienten kommt es zu tödlichen Verläufen, die kongenitale Infektion kann zu Fehlbildungen des fetalen Gehirns führen. LCMV ist außerdem ein wichtiges Modellpathogen für immunologische Studien.
